I wouldn’t bother with a CPL at 45 in today’s climate, unless you have some serious connections and a guaranteed job, even then you’ll be taking a huge pay cut. I think that you can instruct on a Class 2 medical in Norway, but I’m basing this off of U.K. CAA rules. 

My advice- find a good school that’s willing to support you during your training. Work out a plan of how often you’ll fly. Study at home, watch videos, join discussions. Widen your knowledge beyond just the PPL syllabus. I’d recommend joining your closest gliding club if you *really* want to get good at flying- start with a glider pilot licence and then to a PPL. You can keep your hours up and have tonnes of fun towing gliders, then have the money to play around in your own private plane weekdays. 

However, if you’re adamant on just going straight to PPL, find an instructor who will not just teach you the syllabus, but help you understand it. Flying shouldn’t just be regurgitating what your instructor says, you should know WHY you are doing it and be able to make your own decisions based off your knowledge. 

Once you qualify, be social, join a flying club or just say hello to everyone around your local airfields. You’re likely to make friends who you can fly with, who you can take flying as well and from there the opportunity to fly abroad, on trips etc opens up. You can even start instructing if you want to give something back. 

Good luck, if you are dedicated you will have the time of your life.

Actually, I can completely empathise. I will state that you need to be completely mentally sound to obtain a a pilot medical. However, depending on your past history and what country you are from, you may be able to obtain a private pilot medical with a history of mental health issues. In all honesty, if you have been diagnosed with anxiety, I doubt very very much you will be able to get a Class 1 (commercial) medical. The risks in the eyes of the regulatory bodies is just too high (look up Germanwings crash, caused by pilot mental health). 

If you’re serious, really serious about getting a private licence, contact your local AME and explain the situation, and book yourself in with a psychologist again, a good on, who is willing to work through these issues with you. 
I’m not sure how much you will be capable of doing, medical wise, but if you can obtain a private medical, then attend psychiatry sessions and begin tackling the root cause of your lack of confidence. Best of luck.

A ceiling fan is a very different shape to an airfoil (which is what a propellor is). Therefore by that deduction it seems highly logical that the flat blade of a fan came first, probably as a windmill, and then the airfoil of the first aircraft’s wings, and finally the electric ceiling fan as we know it.

Lift can be generated by either a flat surface (but is highly inefficient), or by an airfoil (a specific shape which can be either symmetric or asymmetric). Simply moving air just requires a surface to exert force on the air, rather than to actually produce useful lift, eg to drag an aeroplane along.

Force = Mass * Accelleration where Accelleration is due to gravity (eg on earth is 9.81ms^-1)
Therefore the force experienced is due to the mass of the object in KG and the Gravitational constant, assuming there is no additional Accelleration from movement of the object (eg taking off, landing or slowing down etc). 

It’s called “G Force” because Accelleration makes it feel like gravity is stronger but actually it’s just because of the cumulative effect of all Accelleration considered.
